be.verb type: **linking (copular)** in the core senses — identity, location, existence, occurrence, price (*she is a pediatrician*, *the total was a hundred dollars*) — and **auxiliary** in senses 6–7, building every progressive (*she is working*) and every passive (*the road was repaved*). Stative except the behavior progressive *he is being rude*.
be.transitivity: **intransitive** — *be* never takes an object, only a subject complement, and that complement is obligatory: *the keys are in the drawer*, but ✗ *She is.* outside the existential *There is.*
be.passive: **no** — *be* builds everyone else's passive and has none of its own: ✗ *A pediatrician is been by her.* Copulas and auxiliaries do not passivize.

beat.verb type: **action** — dynamic in every documented sense: defeat, strike repeatedly, throb, whisk, outrun a deadline. The *I'm beat* of sense 9 is an adjective, not a verb form.
beat.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the defeat, hitting, cooking, and get-there-first senses (*we beat Chicago 4-1*, *beat the cream*, *she beat me to the spot*), intransitive of rain, surf, and hearts (*rain beat against the windows*, *my pulse beat faster*).
beat.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the prisoners had been beaten before anyone reached them*, *he looked like he had been beaten up*. No passive of the intransitive *the surf beats on those rocks*.

browbeat.verb type: **action** — dynamic, a verb of verbal pressure. The participle *browbeaten* doubles as an adjective: *he had the browbeaten look of a man who never wins an argument*.
browbeat.transitivity: **transitive** only, with an obligatory human object, typically in the frame *browbeat someone into* doing something: *the attorney browbeat the witness*; ✗ *The attorney browbeat until the judge stepped in.*
browbeat.passive: **yes**, and it is common — *two suppliers had been browbeaten into cutting their prices*; *everyone left the meeting feeling browbeaten*.

carve.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout: shaping wood or stone, slicing meat, incising letters, and the figurative *carve out* / *carve up*. *Carven* is no longer a verb form, only a literary adjective — ✗ *I have carven the turkey*.
carve.transitivity: **both**, but overwhelmingly transitive (*carve a pumpkin*, *carve her initials into the table*, *carve out two hours*); the object drops only in the absolute use *Who carves at your house?*
carve.passive: **yes** — *the turkey had been carved by the time we sat down*, *the old dairy farm was carved up into forty lots*.

forego.verb type: **action** in the literal 'come or go before' sense, though the subject is an event rather than an agent (*months of quiet rehearsal forewent opening night*). What survives in live American English is adjectival: *the foregoing section*, *a foregone conclusion*.
forego.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what the subject precedes: *a hymn would forego the sermon*. No intransitive use; the finite forms are formal and rare either way.
forego.passive: **restricted** — formally possible but effectively unattested (*the sermon was foregone by a hymn* reads as an error for *forgone*); the participle lives on only as the adjective in *a foregone conclusion*.

forgo.verb type: **action** — dynamic, a deliberate choice to do without. *Forgone* also serves as an adjective in the economics sense: *forgone revenue*, *forgone wages*.
forgo.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — *I'll forgo dessert*, *the lender agreed to forgo interest for six months*; ✗ *The lender agreed to forgo.*
forgo.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but stiff and rare (*the bonus was forgone so the team could split it*); American writing keeps it active or reaches for the adjective, *ninety million in forgone revenue*.

go.verb type: **action** — dynamic in the movement, departure, process, and give-out senses (*they went to the coast*, *the transmission went*). Also **linking (copular)** with a bare adjective in *go bad*, *go sour*, *go blind*, *go bankrupt* — almost always a change for the worse.
go.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense the entry documents; destinations, paths, and complements arrive through prepositions or particles (*go to the store*, *go through the file*, *go with those pants*). Even *six goes into forty-eight* is intransitive.
go.passive: **no** — with no object there is nothing to promote: ✗ *The coast was gone to by them*, ✗ *Home had been gone by everyone.* Only the prepositional phrasal *go through* allows a marginal passive in casual speech — *every bag had been gone through*.

shear.verb type: **action** — dynamic. The participle splits by sense: *shorn* for wool, hair, and figurative stripping (*shorn of authority*), *sheared* for metal snapping under load (*the bolt sheared off*).
shear.transitivity: **both** — transitive of animals and hair (*they shear the flock every spring*, *a barber sheared his curls off*), intransitive in the mechanical sense (*a rivet can shear long before it pulls out*).
shear.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses, and often the preferred form — *every animal on the place has been shorn*, *the recruits were shorn the first morning*. *Shorn of* is passive-only: *by 1919 the emperor had been shorn of every real power*. No passive of the intransitive *the bolt sheared off*.

undergo.verb type: **action** — dynamic but non-agentive: the subject is the one something is done to (*the design had undergone six revisions*, *she underwent knee surgery*). No linking or stative use, and it never means physical travel the way *go* does.
undergo.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory, and the object is always a process, treatment, or change: *undergo two weeks of training*, *undergo an ordeal*; ✗ *All new hires undergo.*
undergo.passive: **no** — the subject is already the affected party, so promotion has nowhere to go: ✗ *Knee surgery was undergone by her*, ✗ *Six revisions had been undergone by the design.* Keep it active, or say *she had knee surgery*.
